title: Why Don’t We Talk More About Family Structure in Schooling?
author: Frederick M. Hess and Ian V. Rowe
summary: In this Education Week Q&A, Rick Hess interviews AEI's Ian Rowe about family structure and student outcomes. Rowe and Brad Wilcox analyzed data on about 51,000 children and found that kids in nonintact families were less likely to earn A's and B's, more likely to have behavior or learning problems flagged, and more than twice as likely to be depressed, with family structure predicting these outcomes more strongly than race or poverty. He cautions that the data show correlation, not cause, and urges the NAEP to report family structure like other demographics. Rowe rejects the charge of shaming single parents, argues for teaching the success sequence, and describes the FREE initiative and Agency Curriculum for building student agency. He closes with advice to school leaders that educating is moral formation and values should be chosen deliberately.
points: Rowe's analysis of about 51,000 children found sizable gaps in grades, behavior flags and depression between intact and nonintact families, even after controls.
He urges NAEP to report family structure alongside race, sex and poverty so educators and parents see a major predictor of success.
Rowe stresses that the goal is clarity, not shaming single parents, many of whom support teaching the success sequence.
The FREE pillars of family, religion, education and entrepreneurship underpin a new Agency Curriculum.
His advice to school leaders is to treat education as moral formation and choose values deliberately.
quotes: Kids in nonintact families were 13% less likely to earn A’s and B’s, 47% more likely to have their parents contacted about behavioral or learning problems at school, and more than twice as likely to be depressed. In fact, family structure predicted these outcomes more strongly than race or poverty did.
Our data can’t pinpoint the cause; we can only establish correlation. Two-parent homes seem to offer kids unique benefits.
Every morning, it was clear that kids from stable families were more ready to learn than their peers.
NAEP collects data on students’ race, ethnicity, sex, poverty, and family structure. But only the latter doesn’t appear in the official nation’s report card.

It’s not about shaming single parents. The goal is to provide the public with a clearer picture of how family structure—alongside race, class, and other factors—influences children’s health, academic success, and economic security.
The success sequence has three steps: Finish high school, get a full-time job, and marry before having kids.
School leaders must recognize that educating students is moral formation. If we aren’t intentional about the values we teach, the void will be filled by social media or other influences.
